dawn on: be realized for the first time
typical: it dawned on sb that..., the truth dawned on sb. NOT for: knowing earlier.
It dawned on me that Jo was right.
The truth finally dawned on him.
deal with: verb
take action to solve a problem or handle a task
typical: deal with a problem/a complaint/an issue. NOT for: avoiding.
I'll deal with this.
The council failed to deal with homelessness.
verb
be about a subject (a book or a speech)
typical: a book/article deals with sth. NOT for: writing it.
The book deals with World War II.
The talk dealt with health.
verb
do business with a person or company
typical: deal with a supplier/company. NOT for: fighting.
We deal with several banks.
I don't deal with that firm.
verb
manage or behave towards a person
typical: deal with sb (well/badly). NOT for: avoiding people.
She deals well with angry customers.
How do you deal with rude people?
depend on: be affected or decided by something else
typical: it depends on sth, depend on how/what/whether. NOT for: being independent.
The price depends on the size.
Choosing a bike depends on what you need.
trust someone or something to help or provide for you
typical: depend on sb/sth (for sth). NOT for: being independent.
die down: become less strong, active or violent
typical: die down, the wind/noise/excitement dies down. NOT for: getting stronger.
The gossip will soon die down.
die out: typical: a species/tradition/language dies out. NOT for: dying of one person.
Wild koalas are in danger of dying out.
The old tradition has died out.
dig in: verb
mix something into soil by digging
typical: dig sth in, dig fertilizer into the soil. NOT for: removing from soil.
Dig some fertilizer into the soil first.
She dug in the compost.
verb
push a hard or pointed object into something
typical: dig sth into sth, dig your nails in. NOT for: pulling out.
She dug her fingernails into his arm.
The straps dug in.
verb
prepare to defend your position and not move (a group)
typical: dig in, dig in for a long fight. NOT for: retreating.
The troops dug in for the winter.
Both sides dug in.
verb
start eating eagerly (informal)
typical: Dig in!, dig in to the food. NOT for: waiting to eat.
Dig in, everyone!
We dug in as soon as the food arrived.
dig up: remove something from the ground with a spade
typical: dig sth up, dig up a plant. NOT for: planting.
I'll dig up that plant and move it.
remove the surface of ground or a road
typical: dig up a road/garden. NOT for: repairing.
find hidden or forgotten information by searching
typical: dig up information/dirt/facts. NOT for: hiding facts.
They tried to dig up dirt on him.
dish out: give something to many people, often carelessly
typical: dish out leaflets/advice/punishment. NOT for: being careful.
typical: dish out food/sandwiches. NOT for: eating.
criticize others but not accept criticism (dish it out)
typical: can dish it out but can't take it. NOT for: praising.
He can dish it out but he can't take it.
She dishes it out all the time.
dive in: typical: dive in with sth, dive in (and do sth). NOT for: hesitating.
Harvey dived in with several questions.
do away with: get rid of something or stop using it
typical: do away with rules/jobs/a system. NOT for: introducing.
Robots could do away with boring jobs.
The school did away with uniforms.
typical: do away with sb/yourself. NOT for: saving.
He tried to do away with his rival.
do over: make a place look better by decorating it (especially AmE)
typical: do sth over. NOT for: damaging.
The apartment was done over in Art Deco style.
do something again because it was wrong (AmE)
typical: do sth over. NOT for: doing it right.
You'll have to do it over.
typical: do a house over. NOT for: helping.
typical: do sb over. NOT for: protecting.
He got done over outside the pub.
do up: verb
fasten something
typical: do up a coat/zip/buttons/shoes. NOT for: undoing.
Do up your coat; it's cold.
The skirt does up at the back.
verb
repair or improve an old building or car
typical: do up a house/car/room. NOT for: demolishing.
They did up an old cottage.
He is doing up an old car.
verb
decorate something in a particular style
typical: be done up in sth. NOT for: leaving bare.
The flat was done up in Viennese style.
The room was done up like a ship.
verb
dress yourself in special clothes
typical: do yourself up, be done up. NOT for: dressing casually.
She was all done up for the party.
He did himself up for the wedding.
do without: typical: do without (sth). NOT for: needing.
There's no sugar, so you'll have to do without.
We can do without a carpet.
used to say something is annoying or unwanted
typical: can do without sth. NOT for: wanting.
I can do without all that hassle.
We could do without the noise.
doze off: fall asleep, especially when you did not intend to
typical: doze off in front of TV/in class. NOT for: staying awake.
He dozed off during the film.
drag on: continue for too long (an event or situation)
typical: drag on for hours/years. NOT for: ending quickly.
The court battle could drag on for years.
The meeting dragged on all afternoon.
drag out: make something last longer than necessary
typical: drag sth out. NOT for: shortening.
Neither wanted to drag the divorce out.
pull someone or something out with effort
typical: drag sb/sth out (of sth). NOT for: carrying gently.
They dragged him out of the car.
draw back: move backwards, especially from fear or surprise
typical: draw back in horror/shock/fear. NOT for: moving forward.
decide not to do something because it is risky
typical: draw back from sth. NOT for: going ahead.
The government drew back from its plan.
They drew back at the last minute.
draw up: verb
prepare a written document such as a plan or contract
typical: draw up a list/plan/contract/proposals. NOT for: signing.
Draw up a list of things to do.
The contract was drawn up last year.
verb
arrive and stop (a vehicle)
typical: a car/taxi draws up. NOT for: driving away.
A taxi drew up at the gate.
A bus drew up outside.
verb
move a chair closer
typical: draw up a chair. NOT for: pushing away.
Draw up a chair and join us.
He drew up a stool.
verb
stand straight, showing pride or anger
typical: draw yourself up (to your full height). NOT for: slouching.
She drew herself up to her full height.
He drew himself up proudly.
dream up: think of a plan or idea, especially an unusual one
typical: dream up a scheme/idea/excuse. NOT for: copying.
He kept dreaming up new schemes.
dress down: wear less formal clothes than usual
typical: dress down on Fridays. NOT for: dressing up.
He dressed down for the weekend.
speak angrily to someone about something wrong
typical: dress sb down, a dressing-down. NOT for: praising.
The boss dressed him down in front of everyone.
She was dressed down for being late.
dress up: wear special clothes for fun, or put them on someone
typical: dress up as sth, dress sb up. NOT for: dressing casually.
He dressed up as a gangster.
We dressed him up as a gorilla.
wear more formal clothes than usual
typical: dress up for a party/interview. NOT for: dressing down.
You don't have to dress up.
make something look more attractive or acceptable
typical: dress sth up (as/in sth). NOT for: exposing the truth.
They dressed up the bad news.
He dressed up the lie as a joke.
drift apart: gradually stop having a close relationship
typical: drift apart over the years. NOT for: growing closer.
My college friends and I drifted apart.
drink up: typical: Drink up!, drink up your milk. NOT for: leaving some.
Come on, drink up your milk.
drive off: leave in a car or drive away
typical: drive off, drive off in a car. NOT for: arriving.
He got in and drove off.
She drove off without a word.
force someone to leave or retreat
typical: drive sb/sth off. NOT for: welcoming.
The dog drove off the thieves.
hit the ball to start a hole in golf
typical: drive off at the first tee. NOT for: chip shots.
He drove off at the first hole.
The players drive off in turn.
drop back: move more slowly than others and fall behind
typical: drop back (behind). NOT for: moving ahead.
He dropped back at the first fence.
Ellen dropped behind to tie her shoe.
drop by: typical: drop by (for a chat), drop by sb's house. NOT for: long stays.
Why don't you drop by tomorrow?
She dropped by to say hello.
drop in: typical: drop in (on sb), drop in for tea. NOT for: planned visits.
I'll drop in on you tomorrow.
drop off: typical: drop off (to sleep). NOT for: waking up.
She kept dropping off at her desk.
take someone or something to a place and leave them there
typical: drop sb/sth off. NOT for: picking up.
I'll drop you off on my way home.
She dropped the kids off at school.
fall to a lower level or amount
typical: sales/numbers drop off. NOT for: rising.
The number of graduates dropped off sharply.
drop out: stop taking part in an activity or leave a group
typical: drop out (of sth). NOT for: joining.
Members move away or drop out.
He dropped out of the race.
leave school or university before finishing
typical: drop out of college/school, a dropout. NOT for: graduating.
Bill dropped out of college after a year.
refuse to live in ordinary society
typical: drop out of society. NOT for: fitting in.
In the 60s, many young people dropped out.
He dropped out and joined a commune.
dry out: become or make something completely dry
typical: let sth dry out, dry sth out. NOT for: getting wet.
Never let the soil dry out.
It took ages to dry the kitchen out.
typical: dry out (in a clinic), dry sb out. NOT for: starting to drink.
He's drying out at a private clinic.
dwell on: think or talk for too long about something, especially unpleasant
typical: dwell on the past/a mistake. NOT for: moving on.
I don't want to dwell on that subject.
